item.title: How Competitive Position Shapes Prices and Costs in a Forecast
item.summary: Porter's five forces describe the competitive pressures that decide how much a company can charge and how much it must pay for inputs. An analyst who builds a financial model needs this to set realistic price and margin assumptions rather than assuming past margins will simply continue.

sections.heading: Why a forecaster cares about competition
sections.body_markdown: Think of a stall at a weekend market. If you are the only seller of fresh bread, you can charge a bit more. If ten stalls sell the same loaf, you must cut your price to keep customers. If the flour supplier is the only one nearby and raises his price, your costs go up. A company's **price** is what it charges per unit, and its **cost** is what it pays to make and deliver that unit. The gap between the two is the **margin**. A financial model projects both price and cost, so the analyst must judge whether competition will squeeze or protect that gap.

sections.heading: The five forces and what each one does
sections.body_markdown: Michael Porter's framework lists five pressures on an industry's profitability. **Bargaining power of buyers**: powerful customers (large, concentrated, able to switch easily) force prices down, which lowers margin. **Bargaining power of suppliers**: powerful suppliers (few of them, no good alternatives) charge more for inputs, which raises costs. **Threat of substitutes**: a different product that meets the same need limits how high prices can go, because customers will switch if prices rise too far. **Threat of new entrants**: if it is easy to enter, extra competitors arrive when profits look attractive and push prices down. High barriers to entry (heavy capital needs, strong brands, regulation, scale advantages) protect prices. **Rivalry among existing competitors**: when rivals are many, similar in size, selling look-alike products, in a slow-growing market, or carrying high fixed costs, they tend to compete on price and spend more on marketing, so prices and margins fall. Strong forces mean weak pricing power and cost pressure. Weak forces mean the opposite.

sections.heading: Position within the industry matters too
sections.body_markdown: Two firms in one industry can face the forces very differently. A company with a strong brand, loyal customers, and many small buyers has weak buyer power against it, so it can often raise prices when its costs rise (this is called **passing through** a cost increase). A **low-cost leader** (a firm that produces more cheaply than its rivals through scale or efficiency) can cut prices and still earn a margin. A seller of an undifferentiated commodity to a few large buyers has little room to raise prices, so cost increases come straight out of its margin. Research cited in the sources found that industry conditions explain only a small share of profit differences between firms. The firm's own position and management therefore matter a great deal, and the analyst should not just copy the industry average.

sections.heading: Turning the analysis into model assumptions
sections.body_markdown: In a model, the five forces become judgments about **price per unit** (or price growth) and **cost per unit** (or cost as a percentage of sales). A firm in a favorable position can be modeled with stable or rising prices and gross margins that hold up when input costs rise. A firm in an unfavorable position needs price declines, rising input costs, or both, which means a lower gross margin. The assumptions must also be consistent with each other. A forecast of fast sales growth through aggressive pricing should come with lower margins, and a forecast of very high margins should not assume that rivals and entrants will stay away. Small shifts in price or cost per unit have a large effect on profit because the margin is the thin difference between two big numbers.

worked_example.problem: Brightwave Appliances has sales of 200 million and cost of goods sold (COGS) of 130 million, a gross margin of 35%. An analyst concludes that a few large retail buyers can switch easily between suppliers and that Brightwave's key component supplier has strong pricing power. For next year the analyst assumes unit volume is unchanged, average selling prices fall 3%, and COGS rises 5%. What is the forecast gross margin?
steps: Current gross profit = 200 − 130 = 70 million, so the current gross margin is 70 ÷ 200 = 35.0%.
Buyer power affects price: new sales = 200 × (1 − 0.03) = 194 million (volume is unchanged, so sales fall by the price cut).
Supplier power affects cost: new COGS = 130 × (1 + 0.05) = 136.5 million.
New gross margin = 57.5 ÷ 194. On the BA II Plus press 57.5 ÷ 194 = to get 0.2964, which is 29.64%.
Compare with the current margin: 35.0% − 29.6% is a drop of about 5.4 percentage points, from the two pressures together.
worked_example.answer: The forecast gross margin is about 29.6%, down from 35.0%, because buyer power lowers prices while supplier power raises costs.

formulas.name: Gross margin
formulas.where: Sales is net revenue; COGS is cost of goods sold. Price pressure lowers Sales per unit and input-cost pressure raises COGS per unit, so both reduce this ratio.

formulas.name: Breakeven quantity
formulas.where: Q_BE is the number of units needed to cover all costs; F is total fixed costs; P is the selling price per unit; V is the variable cost per unit. Lower P or higher V makes the denominator smaller and the breakeven quantity larger.

exam_traps: Treating a high-growth or high-margin industry as automatically good for every firm in it: the firm's own competitive position decides whether it can keep the price premium.
Confusing buyer power with supplier power: buyers mainly push selling prices down, while suppliers mainly push input costs up.
Forecasting that all firms in an industry will pass cost increases through to customers equally, ignoring that a differentiated firm can do so far more than a commodity seller.
Forgetting that barriers to entry and weak rivalry protect prices only while they last; assuming current high margins last forever ignores the entry that high profits attract.
Assuming substitutes only matter within the same industry, when the most dangerous substitute is often a different product that meets the same need.

item.stem: A manufacturer sells almost all of its output to three large retailers. Each retailer can move its orders to a competing manufacturer at little cost. Which forecast assumption is most consistent with this competitive position?

options.text: Selling prices will rise, because large orders signal strong demand
options.explanation: Treats customer concentration as a sign of demand strength. Concentrated buyers with low switching costs have bargaining power and push prices down.

options.text: Selling prices will be pushed down, reducing the gross margin
options.explanation: Correct. Powerful buyers who can switch easily can demand lower prices, which squeezes the margin.

options.text: Cost of goods sold will fall, so the gross margin will hold steady
options.explanation: Confuses buyer power with supplier power. Powerful buyers act on the selling price, not on what the firm pays for inputs.

item.stem: A food processor buys a key ingredient from one supplier. No other supplier makes an equivalent ingredient. Which is the most reasonable effect to build into the forecast?

options.text: Selling prices will be forced down by the supplier's demands
options.explanation: Mixes up supplier power and buyer power. A powerful supplier mainly raises the firm's input costs, not its selling price.

options.text: Input costs will fall as the supplier competes for the firm's orders
options.explanation: Reverses the effect. With no alternatives, the supplier is the one with leverage and does not need to compete on price.

options.text: Input costs will rise, and the margin shrinks unless higher costs can be passed on
options.explanation: Correct. Strong supplier power raises input costs, and the margin falls unless the firm can raise its own prices.

item.stem: A firm has fixed costs of 600,000 per year and a variable cost of 30 per unit. It currently sells at 50 per unit. Large customers use their bargaining power to force the price down to 45, with variable cost unchanged. What is the new breakeven quantity? Round to the nearest whole unit.

options.text: 40,000 units
options.explanation: Correct. The unit margin falls to 45 − 30 = 15, so the breakeven quantity is 600,000 ÷ 15 = 40,000 units.

options.text: 30,000 units
options.explanation: Uses the old price of 50 (margin 20), ignoring the price cut that buyer power forced.

options.text: 13,333 units
options.explanation: Divides fixed costs by the price of 45 and forgets to subtract variable cost per unit.

item.stem: A company's product meets a need that a cheaper product from a different industry also meets, and customers can switch to it easily. How does this competitive force most directly affect the company's pricing?

options.text: It does not affect pricing, since substitutes only matter to rivals in the same industry
options.explanation: Misreads the force. Substitutes by definition often come from outside the industry, and they still compete for the same customer need.

options.text: It allows price increases, because the firm's direct competitors are not affected
options.explanation: Ignores that customers can leave the industry entirely. The substitute limits price increases rather than enabling them.

options.text: It caps the price the firm can charge, since higher prices push customers toward the alternative
options.explanation: Correct. The price and performance of a close substitute set a ceiling on what customers will pay.

item.stem: A firm has fixed costs of 600,000 per year and sells at 50 per unit, a price that is unchanged. A powerful supplier raises the firm's variable cost from 30 to 34 per unit. What is the new breakeven quantity? Round to the nearest whole unit.

options.text: 30,000 units
options.explanation: Uses the old variable cost of 30 (margin 20) and ignores the supplier's increase.

options.text: 37,500 units
options.explanation: Correct. The unit margin falls to 50 − 34 = 16, so the breakeven quantity is 600,000 ÷ 16 = 37,500 units.

options.text: 25,000 units
options.explanation: Adds the 4 cost increase to the margin (20 + 4 = 24) instead of subtracting it.

item.stem: An industry is growing slowly. It has many rivals of similar size, high fixed costs, and products that customers see as nearly identical. Which expectation for the typical firm is most reasonable?

options.text: Rivals will avoid price cuts because most of their costs are fixed
options.explanation: Gets the effect of high fixed costs backwards. Firms with high fixed costs are tempted to cut prices to fill capacity and spread those costs.

options.text: Price competition and higher selling costs will pressure margins
options.explanation: Correct. Intense rivalry (many equal rivals, little differentiation, slow growth, high fixed costs) leads to price cuts and more spending on marketing, which lowers margins.

options.text: Margins will widen because rivals will share the market evenly
options.explanation: Assumes an even split removes competition. Similar size and look-alike products make rivalry stronger, not weaker.

item.stem: Input costs rise 6% for every firm in an industry. Firm A has a well-known brand, differentiated products, and many small customers. Firm B sells a commodity product to a few large buyers that can easily switch suppliers. Which forecast is most consistent with the firms' competitive positions?

options.text: Firm A's gross margin roughly holds as it raises prices, while Firm B's margin narrows
options.explanation: Correct. Firm A has weak buyer power against it and can pass the cost increase through. Firm B cannot, so the cost increase reduces its margin.

options.text: Both firms' margins narrow equally, since the cost increase hits the whole industry
options.explanation: Treats the industry as the only driver. Pass-through ability depends on each firm's own position, so effects differ across firms.

options.text: Firm B's margin holds because large buyers commit volume, while Firm A's margin narrows
options.explanation: Reverses the logic. Large buyers with low switching costs have bargaining power and resist price increases, while A's loyal small customers do not.

item.stem: A firm has fixed costs of 600,000 per year. It currently sells at 50 per unit with a variable cost of 30 per unit. Its analyst forecasts that buyer power cuts the price to 46 and supplier power raises the variable cost to 34 per unit. What is the forecast breakeven quantity? Round to the nearest whole unit.

options.text: 37,500 units
options.explanation: Includes only one of the two pressures (price 46 with cost 30, or price 50 with cost 34), giving a margin of 16 instead of 12.

options.text: 30,000 units
options.explanation: Treats the 4 cost increase as offsetting the 4 price cut, so the margin stays at 20, but both changes reduce the margin.

options.text: 50,000 units
options.explanation: Correct. The unit margin is 46 − 34 = 12, so the breakeven quantity is 600,000 ÷ 12 = 50,000 units.

item.front: Which of Porter's five forces mainly pushes a firm's selling prices down, and which mainly pushes its input costs up?
item.back: Bargaining power of buyers pushes selling prices down; bargaining power of suppliers pushes input costs up.

item.front: How do high barriers to entry affect a firm's pricing power?
item.back: They keep new competitors out, which protects prices and margins. Low barriers let new entrants arrive and push prices down.

item.front: Why can two firms in the same industry have different forecast margins when input costs rise?
item.back: Their competitive positions differ. A differentiated firm with weak buyer power can pass costs through; a commodity seller facing strong buyers cannot.

item.front: What does the threat of substitutes do to a firm's pricing?
item.back: It caps the price the firm can charge, because customers switch to the alternative if the price rises too far.

warnings: 1/8 items have the longest option as the key
